title: Olympic Code versus Village Art
bigQuestion: What does a traditional art gain and lose when it rewrites its rules to fit the Olympic stage?

story.title: Two Kinds of Güreş
story.kicker: A family watches wrestling in Edirne and then in Paris a few weeks later, and the same word names two different worlds.
paragraphs: In the summer of 2024, a family from Istanbul sits in the stands at Sarayiçi, a meadow beside the river in Edirne, Turkey. Hundreds of wrestlers in heavy leather trousers wait their turn. Each is shining with olive oil. Drummers and players of the zurna, a loud reed pipe, play as pairs are called onto the field.

This is Kırkpınar, the oil wrestling festival that Edirne holds every summer. The Turkish word for wrestling is güreş. Here the wrestlers are grouped by age and experience, and many bouts run at once on the grass. The grand winner is named başpehlivan, or chief wrestler, and receives a golden belt.

A few weeks later the same family watches the Paris Olympic Games on television. The wrestling is held indoors at the Champ-de-Mars Arena, on a round mat of set size. Each bout has two periods of three minutes. Wrestlers weigh in the morning of competition and compete in fixed weight classes. The Turkish broadcast still calls it güreş.

The grandmother points out that both events use one word. Yet one answers to a city, a festival and centuries of local custom. The other answers to United World Wrestling and the International Olympic Committee. The family wonders what each one had to give up to become what it is.
story.think: If two events share a name but answer to different institutions, are they the same art?

lessons.title: Kırkpınar in Edirne
lessons.mainIdea: Kırkpınar oil wrestling is run by the city of Edirne under local custom, not by an Olympic federation.
reading: *Kırkpınar* is held each summer in Edirne, a city in northwestern Turkey near the borders with Greece and Bulgaria. Its organizers trace the festival to the 1300s, in the early Ottoman period. That founding date rests on tradition and a legend about forty soldiers, not on a record from the time. Documents show the festival well established by the Ottoman centuries that followed.

Wrestlers wear the *kispet*, heavy trousers made of water buffalo or calf leather. They coat themselves with olive oil before bouts. Wrestlers are grouped by age and experience rather than by body weight on a scale. The top class competes for the title of başpehlivan and a golden belt.

The festival has its own officials and ceremonies. An announcer called the cazgır introduces wrestlers in rhymed verse. The Edirne city government runs the event. In 2010 UNESCO added the Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival to its Representative List of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage* of Humanity.

words.d: an oil wrestling festival held every summer in Edirne, Turkey, and traced by tradition to the 1300s
the heavy leather trousers worn in Turkish oil wrestling
living customs, arts and festivals that UNESCO lists as important to protect

lessons.title: Naadam and Mongolian Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: Mongolian wrestling at the Naadam festival keeps its own titles and customs, including traditionally having no weight classes.
reading: *Naadam* is Mongolia's national summer festival, held each year in July. Its three main contests are wrestling, horse racing and archery, often called the three games of men. The national Naadam in Ulaanbaatar opens on July 11, the date of the 1921 revolution. Towns and districts across the country hold their own Naadam as well.

Mongolian wrestling, called bökh, traditionally has no weight classes. A small wrestler may meet a very large one. Wrestlers wear the zodog, a short jacket open across the chest, and the shuudag, tight briefs. A popular story says the jacket is open because a woman once entered in disguise and won. That tale is a legend, not a dated record.

Winners earn state titles named after strong animals, such as arslan, meaning lion. The highest title is avarga, often translated as titan. Before and after bouts, wrestlers perform an eagle dance, described by many Mongolians as a show of honor. In 2010 UNESCO listed Naadam as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

words.d: Mongolia's national summer festival, with wrestling, horse racing and archery
Mongolian wrestling, traditionally held with no weight classes
an honor name given to a winner, such as arslan (lion) in Mongolian wrestling

lessons.title: Schwingen in the Sawdust
lessons.mainIdea: Swiss schwingen answers to a national wrestling association and a festival held every three years, with a live bull as a prize.
reading: Schwingen is a style of wrestling from the Swiss Alps and the lands around them. Bouts take place in a ring of sawdust. Each wrestler wears short canvas trousers pulled over regular clothes. Wrestlers traditionally shake hands before a bout, and the winner brushes sawdust from the loser's back after it.

The Unspunnen festival near Interlaken, first held in 1805, helped make schwingen a national symbol. The Federal Wrestling Association, or Eidgenössischer Schwingerverband, was founded in 1895. It runs the *Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival*, held every three years. Hundreds of thousands of people visit the festival grounds.

Schwingen has no weight classes. The overall winner is named Schwingerkönig, or king of the schwingers. The main prize is a live bull, a reminder of the art's farming roots. Schwingen is not part of the Olympic Games. Its rules answer to a Swiss association, not to an international federation.

the Swiss national schwingen festival, held every three years
a custom, object or image that people use to stand for their country

lessons.title: Judo Comes to Tokyo, 1964
lessons.mainIdea: Judo joined the Olympic Games at Tokyo in 1964 with weight classes, and a Dutch champion's win changed who owned the sport.
reading: The *International Judo Federation*, or IJF, was founded in 1951. Its members were national judo bodies from several countries. When Tokyo won the 1964 Olympic Games, Japan pushed to add judo. The Nippon Budokan hall was built in Tokyo for the judo events. Judo became the first Asian martial art on the Olympic program.

Kodokan judo had no weight classes in its early decades. A small player might face a large one. For Tokyo 1964, organizers set up four divisions: lightweight, middleweight, heavyweight and an open class for all sizes. This *weight class* system followed Western wrestling and boxing, which already used them.

Japanese players won three of the four events. In the open class, Anton Geesink of the Netherlands defeated Kaminaga Akio before a crowd at the Budokan. Many in Japan felt shock. Geesink's win showed that judo was now a world sport, and that its rules would be set by an international federation, not by Tokyo alone.

words.d: the IJF, founded in 1951, which sets judo's international competition rules
a division in which competitors must weigh within set limits
a division open to competitors of any weight

lessons.title: A Blue Jacket and a Clock
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic judo changed its uniforms and timing so audiences could follow it, which some traditional teachers opposed.
reading: Judo left the program at Mexico City in 1968 and returned at Munich in 1972. It has been at every Summer Games since. Women's judo appeared as a demonstration event at Seoul in 1988. It became a full medal sport at Barcelona in 1992. Today men and women each have seven Olympic weight classes.

In the 1990s the IJF approved a blue *judogi*, the judo uniform, for one athlete in each match. The other athlete wears white. Blue jackets were first used at the Olympics in Sydney in 2000. Anton Geesink had argued for them so referees, judges and TV viewers could tell the two players apart. The Kodokan and many Japanese teachers opposed the change, preferring the white judogi alone.

The IJF also controls the clock and the cloth. Since 2017, regular time for Olympic judo bouts has been four minutes for both men and women. If the score is tied, a *golden score* period continues until someone scores. The IJF also approves which uniforms may be worn at its events, with labels showing they meet its rules.

an extra period in judo that ends as soon as either athlete scores
to make things follow one fixed set of rules or sizes everywhere

lessons.title: Taekwondo and Electronic Scoring
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic taekwondo adopted electronic scoring vests to answer judging disputes, reshaping the sport around a sensor.
reading: Taekwondo appeared as a demonstration sport at the 1988 Seoul Olympics and again at Barcelona in 1992. It became a full medal sport at Sydney in 2000. The Olympic program has four weight classes for men and four for women, fewer than the eight each at world championships. So some athletes must move up or down a class to reach the Games.

Early Olympic taekwondo relied on corner judges pressing buttons to award points. Disputed decisions caused protests, including at the 2008 Beijing Games. World Taekwondo, then named the World Taekwondo Federation, responded with electronic scoring. At the London Olympics in 2012, athletes wore a *protector and scoring system*, or PSS, with sensors in the vest and foot socks.

Instant video replay was also added so coaches could challenge calls. These tools made scoring more open to review. They also changed what counted as a scoring contact. The sport on the Olympic mat now answers to a rule book and a sensor. A local school's sparring rules, set by its own teachers, answer to no such *technology*.

words.d: PSS, electronic vests and sensors used to score Olympic taekwondo since London 2012
a recording that officials watch again to review a disputed call

lessons.title: Two Styles in the Rule Book
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic wrestling uses two styles, Greco-Roman and freestyle, each shaped by nineteenth- and twentieth-century rule makers.
reading: Wrestling was on the program of the ancient Olympic Games, starting in 708 BCE by tradition. The modern Games of 1896 in Athens held one wrestling event. It followed a style developed in nineteenth-century France and later called *Greco-Roman*. Despite the name, it was a modern style, not a copy of ancient Greek wrestling. Its rules ban holds below the waist.

Freestyle wrestling grew from catch-as-catch-can wrestling in Britain and the United States. It first appeared at the Olympics in St. Louis in 1904, where every entrant was American. The international federation now called United World Wrestling was founded in 1912. It was long known by its French initials, FILA, and took its current name in 2014.

Women's freestyle wrestling joined the Olympics at Athens in 2004. In February 2013, the IOC's executive board recommended dropping wrestling from future Games. Wrestling bodies changed leaders and rules, and in September 2013 the IOC voted to keep the sport. The episode showed that even the oldest Olympic sport stays only as long as the IOC agrees.

words.d: an Olympic wrestling style from nineteenth-century France that bans holds below the waist
an Olympic wrestling style that grew from catch-as-catch-can wrestling in Britain and the United States
the international wrestling federation, founded in 1912 and known as FILA until 2014

lessons.title: Karate's Single Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Karate was an Olympic sport only at Tokyo 2020, and fitting it in meant merging classes and choosing one federation's rules.
reading: Karate began on Okinawa and spread to mainland Japan in the 1920s. By the late 1900s, it had many styles and many associations. The World Union of Karate-do Organizations formed in 1970 to run world championships. It later became the *World Karate Federation*, or WKF, which the IOC recognized as karate's international federation.

Tokyo won the 2020 Games, and karate was added as a host-city sport. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Games were held in 2021. Karate took place at the Nippon Budokan. There were two disciplines: *kata*, solo forms judged by a panel, and kumite, scored bouts. Olympic kumite had three weight classes per sex, merged from the five used at WKF world championships.

Karate was not kept for Paris 2024 or Los Angeles 2028. Some karate teachers said the Olympic format favored one federation's rules over the many styles. Others said the Games brought karate new attention. Under IOC rules, a host city may propose extra sports, so an art's Olympic place can depend on who hosts.

words.d: the WKF, the international karate body recognized by the IOC
a set series of karate movements performed alone and judged by a panel in competition
a sport added to one Olympic Games at the request of the city hosting it

lessons.title: Wushu Outside the Rings
lessons.mainIdea: China built competition wushu as a state sport with set routines, and it has sought Olympic status without gaining it.
reading: China has many local martial traditions, each tied to a region, a family or a village. After 1949, the People's Republic of China set up a state sports system. In the 1950s its sports officials created standard *wushu* routines for competition. Judges scored routines for form and difficulty, much like gymnastics.

The International Wushu Federation, or IWUF, was founded in 1990. Competition wushu has two main parts. Taolu are set routines, with or without weapons. Sanda, also called sanshou, is scored full-contact bouts. Wushu has been on the Asian Games program since Beijing hosted in 1990.

China asked to add wushu to the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The IOC did not make it a medal sport. Instead, it allowed a separate Beijing 2008 Wushu Tournament during the Games. Many older family and village styles do not fit either taolu or sanda. So the *state* version of wushu and the local styles answer to different institutions.

words.d: a Chinese word for martial arts; also the name of China's state competition sport
set routines in competition wushu, judged for form and difficulty
a government and its offices, such as a national sports ministry

lessons.title: Muay Thai: Stadiums and Temple Fairs
lessons.mainIdea: Muay Thai moved from temple fairs to Bangkok stadiums with gloves and rings, then built an amateur federation seeking Olympic status.
reading: For centuries, boxing bouts in Siam, now Thailand, took place at temple fairs and festivals. Fighters wrapped their hands in rope or cloth. In the 1920s and 1930s, Bangkok rings began requiring gloves and set rounds, borrowed from Western boxing. Rajadamnern Stadium opened in 1945. Lumpinee Stadium, run by the Royal Thai Army, opened in 1956.

Before a bout, fighters perform the *wai khru*, a ritual of respect to teachers, and a dance called ram muay. Many wear a headband called the mongkhon, which the fighter's teacher places and removes. Musicians play a pipe and drums during the bout. These customs stayed in the stadium even as the rules changed.

In 1992 the International Federation of Muaythai Associations, or *IFMA*, was founded to run amateur competition. Amateur rules add protective gear and shorter bouts. The IOC gave IFMA provisional recognition in 2016 and full recognition in 2021. Recognition is a step toward the Olympic program, but it does not guarantee a place at the Games.

lessons.title: The IOC's Power to Recognize
lessons.mainIdea: The IOC recognizes one international federation per sport, and it can withdraw that recognition, as it did with boxing in 2023.
reading: The *Olympic Charter* is the IOC's founding rule book. It says the IOC recognizes international federations to govern their sports at the world level. Normally the IOC recognizes one federation for each sport. That federation writes the competition rules and runs qualifying events for the Games.

Boxing has been on the Olympic program since St. Louis in 1904, except in 1912. For decades, its federation was known as AIBA, later renamed the International Boxing Association, or IBA. The IOC raised concerns about its judging, finances and leadership. It suspended the federation in 2019 and ran the boxing events itself at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.

In June 2023 the IOC withdrew its *recognition* of the IBA altogether. A new body, World Boxing, was founded in 2023. The IOC recognized World Boxing in 2025 and kept boxing on the program for Los Angeles 2028. A sport's Olympic place depends on its federation keeping the IOC's trust.

words.d: the IOC's founding rule book, which sets out how the Olympic movement is governed
formal approval by a higher body, such as the IOC approving a federation
a world body that governs one sport and writes its competition rules

lessons.title: UNESCO and a Different Kind of Value
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's heritage lists value martial traditions as living culture, which is a different kind of recognition from the Olympic path.
reading: In 2003 UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, often called the *Intangible Heritage Convention*. It asks countries to protect living customs, such as music, crafts, festivals and games. Countries nominate traditions for UNESCO's lists. The lists do not set rules for competition. They honor a practice's place in the life of a community.

Several martial traditions are on the lists. The Korean art of taekkyeon was listed in 2011. The capoeira circle of Brazil, the roda, was listed in 2014. In 2018, North and South Korea jointly nominated ssireum, Korean wrestling, the first such joint listing by the two countries. In 2019 UNESCO listed pencak silat from Indonesia and silat from Malaysia as separate entries.

Olympic recognition and UNESCO listing reward different things. The Olympic path rewards a single international rule book, weight classes and a clock. The UNESCO path rewards *safeguarding*, keeping a practice alive with its music, clothing and local meanings. An art can pursue both, but each answers to a different institution with different goals.
